questions.q: Per this lesson, how does governance differ from administration?
options: They are identical terms for the same work
Governance is the decision rights and policy framework for how platform decisions get made; administration is the day-to-day work of running the platform within that framework
Administration only applies to developers, while governance only applies to admins
Governance is a Salesforce product feature, while administration is a manual process
questions.explain: Governance sets the decision rights and standards; administration is the hands-on daily work (creating users, building Flows) carried out within that framework.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of tactical governance, per this lesson's three-layer model?
options: An executive steering committee setting the platform's multi-year roadmap
A developer writing a single Apex trigger
An admin reviewing one specific change request against existing standards
A Center of Excellence defining the org's data model standards and naming conventions
questions.explain: Tactical governance translates strategy into enforceable standards and policy — exactly the layer where a Center of Excellence typically operates, as described in this lesson.

questions.q: What is the main job of a Center of Excellence (CoE), as this lesson describes it?
options: To own the platform's standards, review significant changes for consistency, and act as the escalation point when teams disagree about how something should be built
To personally build every customization the organization needs
To replace the need for any change advisory board
To approve every individual user's login request
questions.explain: The CoE's job, per this lesson, is to make sure everyone building on the platform pulls in the same direction by owning standards and resolving disagreements — not to do all the building itself.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the risk of a fully federated governance model with no real central enforcement?
options: There is no risk — federation always improves consistency automatically
It becomes identical to a fully centralized model
It becomes indistinguishable from plain decentralization, reproducing the inconsistency and technical-debt problems governance exists to prevent
It eliminates the need for any standards at all, which is desirable
questions.explain: The lesson warns that federation without real enforcement of central standards just becomes decentralization with no oversight, reproducing the org-wide inconsistency governance is meant to solve.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a governance charter accomplishes little on its own, once written?
options: Because governance charters are legally invalid in most jurisdictions
Because only developers are allowed to read governance documents
Because charters should be rewritten from scratch every single week
Because governance only works as a continuously running program — standards have to actually be enforced through change control, review boards, and kept-current documentation, not just filed away
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes governance as an ongoing program: a charter that isn't connected to active enforcement mechanisms like change control, review boards, and current documentation is just a stale document nobody consults.
